# The Archive of Disappearing Sounds

Marta's job is to record things going extinct.

Not animals — though she once spent three weeks in a marsh waiting for a corncrake that never called — but sounds. The institute where she works keeps a library of noises slipping out of the world: the mechanical shutter of a film camera, the ring of a rotary telephone, the cough and whir of a dot-matrix printer. When a sound's last natural habitat disappears — the last factory floor with pneumatic presses, the last cinema running a carbon-arc projector — someone has to kneel down with a microphone and catch it before it goes.

People assume the archive is nostalgic. It isn't, exactly. Nostalgia wants the past back; Marta only wants it witnessed. There's a difference between missing a sound and refusing to let it vanish unrecorded.

Her favorite recordings are the ones nobody thinks to save. A pencil sharpener bolted to a wall, cranked by a child. An ice cream truck playing a warped tape of "Turkey in the Straw." The heavy clunk of a payphone receiver hung back on its hook. The collection holds drawers of doorbells, a shelf of school bells from towns that consolidated their schools decades ago, a box labeled simply *cash registers, mechanical*. She recorded the last hand-cranked elevator in her city before the building was renovated — the operator, an old man named Ferenc, let her ride up and down for an hour while he talked about his forty years in the cage, and underneath his voice you can hear the cables singing.

Sound is the most perishable art. A painting hangs for centuries. A book outlives its language. But a sound exists only while it's happening, and then it's gone, unless someone stood nearby with a machine and caught it.

Lately she's been thinking about voices.

The archive has recordings of the last speakers of dying languages — there's a famous one, a man in Australia taped in the 1970s, singing songs no one else on earth could understand even as he sang them. Marta has listened to those reels hundreds of times. What moves her isn't the words. It's the pauses. The way he breathes between phrases. You can hear him deciding how to say something, weighing it, the way all speakers do, in a language that will outlive him by exactly the length of the tape.

Visitors come through sometimes. A young composer who samples the tapes, hunting for textures. A conservator who spends weeks restoring a degraded recording of foghorns. And once, an old man who asked to hear a steam whistle — just once more, he said, while his hearing was still good enough to hold it. Marta played it for him in the listening booth. He sat very straight with his eyes closed, and when it ended he thanked her as if she'd done something intimate, which, she supposed, she had.

Last spring her father had surgery. Nothing dramatic — they said so themselves, routine — but Marta drove to the hospital with her field recorder in her bag, and while he dozed off the anesthesia in recovery, she sat beside him and turned it on. Just for a minute. His breathing. The small wet sounds of a sleeping mouth. A nurse's shoes squeaking somewhere far away.

He woke and said, "You're always listening to something," which was true, and not a compliment, and she said, "Occupational habit," and he laughed, and she didn't record the laugh because the recorder was already off, and she has regretted that ever since — not because the laugh was precious, but because switching it off was a decision, and decisions are the one thing the archive cannot hold.

In June he died. Not of anything the surgery touched. The body keeps its own schedule and doesn't file reports.

Now she plays the recovery-room tape more than she should. Ninety-one seconds. His breath going in and out, unhurried, trusting. In the background, a heart monitor she didn't notice at the time, keeping its small steady time like a metronome for a piece too slow to finish.

Here is what she has learned in ten years of kneeling near dying sounds: the microphone keeps everything except meaning. Play her father's breathing to a stranger and they hear an old man sleeping. Play it to her and she hears the Tuesday afternoon when she almost lost him and didn't know yet that losing was merely postponed. The waveform is identical. The archive stores the sound. The listening is not transferable.

This is the flaw in her life's work, and she suspects the institute knows it, though no one says it aloud. They are building a library of shells. Every recording is a shell — perfect, exact, empty of the listener who gave it weight. Somewhere in the vaults sit four hundred hours of steam locomotives, and every hour of it is dead to anyone who never stood on a platform at six in the morning and felt the whistle arrive in the chest before the ears.

Sometimes, between assignments, she records room tone. Thirty seconds of an empty studio, an empty kitchen, an empty church. Silence, properly captured, turns out not to be silent at all — it hums, it settles, it carries the ghost of whatever happened there an instant ago. She files these under a category of her own invention: *rooms pretending nothing is happening.*

Still, she goes to work. Still, she packs the microphones and the windshields and the spare batteries and drives to wherever a sound is in its last season. Last month it was a bell foundry closing after a hundred and forty years. She recorded the pour, the mold room, the cooling. The founder — a woman with burn-scarred forearms — let her strike the final bell before it shipped, and Marta held the microphone so close her own hands rang.

On the tape, beneath the bell's long bronze decay, you can hear Marta exhale. She has decided to leave it in. Some archivist a century from now will wonder about that breath — whether it was grief or relief or just the ordinary air of a person standing inside a moment, trying to keep it.

It was all three. But that part doesn't survive the transfer. It never does. Which is why someone has to keep standing next to the sounds while they're still happening — not to save them, exactly, but to prove that somebody, once, was near enough to listen.
